ap_physics_1-m03.set_intro: A student measures the gauge pressure at several depths in an open tank that contains a liquid of constant density. The table shows the measurements.

stimulus.description: Gauge pressure at different depths in an open tank of a liquid

items.stem: What is the density of the liquid?

options.why: Divides the pressure by the depth and does not divide by the acceleration due to gravity.
The gauge pressure is $\rho gd$, so $\rho=P/(gd)$; every row gives about $1260\text{ kg/m}^3$ (for example $74100\text{ Pa}/(9.8\times6\text{ m})$).
Divides the pressure at the deepest point by the depth and by $g$ but forgets to convert kilopascals to pascals.
Multiplies the pressure by the depth and divides by $g$.

blueprint.subject: ap_physics_1
blueprint.concept: Two questions about a table of gauge pressure versus depth in a liquid
student_thinking: Use the gauge pressure $\rho gd$ to find the density from one row
Extend the linear relationship to a greater depth and add the atmospheric pressure

key_conditions.condition: the liquid is at rest with constant density
key_conditions.evidence: the shared stimulus describes an open tank of a liquid

misconceptions.description: Divides the pressure by the depth and does not divide by the acceleration due to gravity.
Divides the pressure at the deepest point by the depth and by $g$ but forgets to convert kilopascals to pascals.
Multiplies the pressure by the depth and divides by $g$.

verification.independent_path: a least-squares slope through the origin and the mean of the ratios P over d agree on the density within two percent

items.stem: The tank is open to the atmosphere, where the pressure is $101\text{ kPa}$. What is the absolute pressure at a depth of $12\text{ m}$?

options.why: Uses the square of the ratio of the depths when extending the gauge pressure, and adds the atmospheric pressure.
The gauge pressure increases linearly with the depth: at $12\text{ m}$ it is $\rho g h/1000=148\text{ kPa}$, so the absolute pressure is $148+101=249\text{ kPa}$.
Gives only the gauge pressure at the depth and leaves out the atmospheric pressure.
Adds the atmospheric pressure to the pressure at the deepest tabulated depth and does not extend to the new depth.

student_thinking: Use the gauge pressure $\rho gd$ to find the density from one row
Extend the linear relationship to a greater depth and add the atmospheric pressure

key_conditions.condition: the liquid is at rest with constant density
key_conditions.evidence: the shared stimulus describes an open tank of a liquid

misconceptions.description: Uses the square of the ratio of the depths when extending the gauge pressure, and adds the atmospheric pressure.
Adds the atmospheric pressure to the pressure at the deepest tabulated depth and does not extend to the new depth.
Gives only the gauge pressure at the depth and leaves out the atmospheric pressure.

verification.independent_path: a least-squares slope through the origin and the mean of the ratios P over d agree on the density within two percent

ap_physics_1-m04.set_intro: A wheel with a moment of inertia of $2\text{ kg m}^2$ rotates about a fixed axle. The graph shows the angular speed of the wheel as a function of time.

stimulus.description: Angular speed of the wheel versus time

items.stem: The wheel always rotates in the same direction. Which statement about the net torque on the wheel from $t=4\text{ s}$ to $t=8\text{ s}$ is correct and best justified?

options.text: The net torque is negative, because the line on the graph does not rise.
options.why: Takes a graph that does not rise to mean a negative torque, but a negative torque would make the angular speed decrease.

options.text: The net torque is not zero, because the wheel keeps turning at $4\text{ rad/s}$ and a torque is needed to keep it turning.
options.why: Thinks that a net torque is needed to maintain a constant angular speed, but a net torque produces an angular acceleration.

options.text: The net torque is zero, because the angular speed is constant and so the angular acceleration is zero.
options.why: The graph is horizontal between $4\text{ s}$ and $8\text{ s}$, so $\alpha=0$ and $\tau_{net}=I\alpha=0$.

options.text: The net torque is $2\text{ N m}$ in the direction of the rotation, because it is the same as in the first segment.
options.why: Carries the net torque of the first segment into the second segment although the slope of the graph is zero there.

blueprint.subject: ap_physics_1
blueprint.concept: Justifying a zero net torque from a constant angular speed on a graph
student_thinking: Read the slope of the graph in the interval
Relate the slope, the angular acceleration and the net torque

key_conditions.condition: the wheel rotates about a fixed axis
key_conditions.evidence: the shared stimulus describes a wheel with an angular speed graph

misconceptions.description: Takes a graph that does not rise to mean a negative torque, but a negative torque would make the angular speed decrease.
Thinks that a net torque is needed to maintain a constant angular speed, but a net torque produces an angular acceleration.
Carries the net torque of the first segment into the second segment although the slope of the graph is zero there.

verification.independent_path: the slope of each segment is computed exactly and by numerical differentiation

items.stem: Which statement about the angle through which the wheel turns from $t=0$ to $t=10\text{ s}$ is correct and best justified?

options.text: The wheel turns through $16\text{ rad}$, because the angle is found only from the part of the graph where the speed is constant.
options.why: Uses only the horizontal part of the graph and leaves out the other segments.

options.text: The wheel turns through $28\text{ rad}$, because the angle is the area under the angular speed-time graph.
options.why: The areas of the segments are 8.00, 16.0 and 4.00 rad, which add to $28.0\text{ rad}$.

options.text: The wheel turns through $40\text{ rad}$, because the angle is the largest angular speed times the total time.
options.why: Uses the largest angular speed for the whole time, but the speed is lower for part of the time.

options.text: The wheel turns through $0\text{ rad}$, because the angle is the slope of the graph.
options.why: Mistakes the slope, which is the angular acceleration, for the angle that the wheel turns.

blueprint.subject: ap_physics_1
blueprint.concept: Justifying the angle turned from the area under an angular speed-time graph
student_thinking: Recognize that the angle is the area under the angular speed-time graph
Add the areas of the three segments

key_conditions.condition: the wheel always turns in the same direction
key_conditions.evidence: the shared stimulus says the wheel always rotates in the same direction

misconceptions.description: Uses only the horizontal part of the graph and leaves out the other segments.
Uses the largest angular speed for the whole time, but the speed is lower for part of the time.
Mistakes the slope, which is the angular acceleration, for the angle that the wheel turns.

verification.independent_path: exact fractions for the areas versus numpy integration of a dense resampling
